* * * **Prime Minister before election** [Jean Chrétien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Chr%C3%A9tien "Jean Chrétien") [Liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_of_Canada "Liberal Party of Canada")**Prime Minister after election** [Jean Chrétien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Chr%C3%A9tien "Jean Chrétien") [Liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_of_Canada "Liberal Party of Canada")

The **2000 Canadian federal election** was held on November 27, 2000, to elect members to the [House of Commons of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_Canada "House of Commons of Canada") of the [37th Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/37th_Canadian_Parliament "37th Canadian Parliament") of [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"). [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Canada "Prime Minister of Canada")[Jean Chrétien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Chr%C3%A9tien "Jean Chrétien")'s [Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_of_Canada "Liberal Party of Canada") won a third [majority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority_government "Majority government").

Since the [previous election of 1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Canadian_federal_election "1997 Canadian federal election"), [small-c conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small-c_conservative "Small-c conservative") had begun attempts to merge the [Reform Party of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Party_of_Canada "Reform Party of Canada") and the [Progressive Conservative Party of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Conservative_Party_of_Canada "Progressive Conservative Party of Canada") as part of the [United Alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Alternative "United Alternative") agenda. During that time, [Jean Charest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Charest "Jean Charest") stepped down as leader of the Progressive Conservatives and former [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Canada "Prime Minister of Canada")[Joe Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Clark "Joe Clark") took over the party and opposed any union with the Reform Party. In the spring of 2000, the Reform Party became the [Canadian Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Alliance "Canadian Alliance"), a political party dedicated to uniting conservatives together into one party. Former Reform Party leader [Preston Manning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preston_Manning "Preston Manning") lost in [a leadership race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Alliance_leadership_elections#2000_leadership_election "Canadian Alliance leadership elections") to [Stockwell Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockwell_Day "Stockwell Day") who became leader of the new Canadian Alliance party.

The federal government called an [early election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snap_election "Snap election") after being in office for close to three and a half years (with a maximum allowed mandate of five years). The governing Liberal Party of Canada won a third consecutive majority government, winning more seats than in 1997. The Canadian Alliance only made minor gains, and an [Eastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Canada "Eastern Canada") breakthrough did not happen. The [Bloc Québécois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloc_Qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois "Bloc Québécois"), [New Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democratic_Party "New Democratic Party") and the [Progressive Conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Conservative_Party_of_Canada "Progressive Conservative Party of Canada") all suffered slight losses.

The Liberal win made Chrétien the first Canadian prime minister to lead his party to three or more consecutive majority governments since [Wilfrid Laurier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilfrid_Laurier "Wilfrid Laurier") in [1908](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_Canadian_federal_election "1908 Canadian federal election"). This was the most recent election as of 2026 in which an incumbent government successfully defended its parliamentary majority. It was also the last election until [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Canadian_federal_election "2025 Canadian federal election") in which a single party won more than 40% of the popular vote. This was the only election contested by the Canadian Alliance and the last by the Progressive Conservatives (as they both merged into the [Conservative Party of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada "Conservative Party of Canada") in 2003). This was the first election in which [Nunavut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nunavut "Nunavut") participated as a separate territory, having previously been part of the [Northwest Territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Territories "Northwest Territories").

## Campaign

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2000_Canadian_federal_election&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section's source code: Campaign")]

On October 22, 2000, [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Canada "Prime Minister of Canada") and Liberal Party leader [Jean Chrétien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Chr%C3%A9tien "Jean Chrétien") advised [Governor General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_General_of_Canada "Governor General of Canada")[Adrienne Clarkson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Clarkson "Adrienne Clarkson") to dissolve parliament and call an [election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snap_election "Snap election") scheduled for November 27, 2000. This move has been viewed by commentators as an attempt to stem a possible rise of support to the newly formed Canadian Alliance, to stop the leadership ambitions of [Paul Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Martin "Paul Martin"), and to capitalize on the nostalgia created by the recent death of [Pierre Trudeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau "Pierre Trudeau"). At the time of the election, the Canadian economy was strong and there were few immediate negative issues, as the opposition parties were not prepared for the campaign.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-3)

The major issue in the election was [health care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_care "Health care") which had risen in public opinion polls to be the most important issue for Canadians.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._122-4)

The public was largely uninterested in the election, with commentators stating that voters expected a repeat of previous regionally divided elections that offered little chance of a change of government.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-5)

The Liberals' final television advertisement, according to [Stephen Clarkson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Clarkson "Stephen Clarkson")'s _[The Big Red Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen\_Clarkson#Bibliography "Stephen Clarkson")_, "emphasized the contrast between [the Liberals and the Canadian Alliance] while warning voters about [PC leader] Joe Clark's claim that he would form a coalition with the Bloc Québécois in a minority government. The ad told Canadians not to take risks with other parties but to choose a strong, proven team".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-6)

### Liberal Party

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2000_Canadian_federal_election&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section's source code: Liberal Party")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Liberal_Party_of_Canada_L_logo-Parti_Liberal_du_Canada_logo_de_L_%281990s-2004%29.svg/250px-Liberal_Party_of_Canada_L_logo-Parti_Liberal_du_Canada_logo_de_L_%281990s-2004%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Liberal_Party_of_Canada_L_logo-Parti_Liberal_du_Canada_logo_de_L_(1990s-2004).svg)

Liberal Party logo during the election.

The [Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_of_Canada "Liberal Party of Canada") entered the election with a record of ending the budgetary deficit, making major reductions in federal spending (such as by cuts to the civil service, privatization of crown corporations), creating new environmental regulations, and increasing spending beginning on social programs beginning in 1998 after the budget deficit had ended and a surplus had been achieved.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._16-7) The Liberal Party came under attack by opposition parties for irregularities in the Department of Human Resources' Transition Job Fund program, but Chrétien managed to capably defend the government's actions.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._16-7) Chrétien was directly attacked by the opposition parties for alleged corrupt involvement from the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) in providing funding to local projects in Chrétien's riding of [Saint-Maurice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Maurice_(federal_electoral_district) "Saint-Maurice (federal electoral district)").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-8) The Liberal Party focused its attacks on the Canadian Alliance, accusing it of being a dangerous right-wing movement that was a threat to national unity.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-9) The Liberal Party's most tense problem was the ongoing leadership feud within the Liberal Party between Chrétien and Finance Minister [Paul Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Martin "Paul Martin") who wanted to replace Chrétien as Liberal leader and Prime Minister.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._115-10)

#### Strategy

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2000_Canadian_federal_election&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section's source code: Strategy")]

Due to the regionalized nature of previous elections, the Liberal Party designed its election strategy along regional lines, aiming to take every seat in Ontario, winning seats in Quebec from the Bloc Québécois, and winning seats in Atlantic Canada, while attempting to minimize losses in [Western Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Canada "Western Canada") to the Canadian Alliance.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._16-7)

Chrétien only spent parts of nine days campaigning in the West, including only two stops in the province of [Alberta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberta "Alberta"), both in the city of [Edmonton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonton "Edmonton") while visiting the province of [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia") only three times, and only in the cities of Victoria and [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-11)

The Liberal Party focused its effort in regaining support in [Atlantic Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Canada "Atlantic Canada"), where the party had suffered serious losses in the 1997 election to the New Democratic Party and Progressive Conservative Party due to the Liberal government's imposition of quotas on Atlantic Canadian cod fisheries and the government's cuts to unemployment insurance benefits.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._20-12) Chrétien gained support during the campaign from former New Brunswick Premier [Frank McKenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_McKenna "Frank McKenna") and former Chrétien government minister and then the current Premier of [Newfoundland and Labrador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newfoundland_and_Labrador "Newfoundland and Labrador"), [Brian Tobin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Tobin "Brian Tobin") resigned as Premier and ran as a Liberal Party candidate in his province.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._20-12) During the campaign, Chrétien apologized to Atlantic Canadians for the negative impact of employment insurance reforms which had caused hardship in Atlantic Canada.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._20-12)

In Quebec, the Liberal Party benefited from the collapse of support for the Progressive Conservative Party, after the PCs' popular [Québécois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French-speaking_Quebecer "French-speaking Quebecer") leader [Jean Charest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Charest "Jean Charest") had resigned in 1998 and was replaced by former Prime Minister [Joe Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Clark "Joe Clark") who was unpopular in Quebec which resulted in three PC members from Quebec defecting to join the Liberal Party prior to the election.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-13) In Quebec the recently passed [Clarity Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarity_Act "Clarity Act") by the federal government was controversial in that it demanded a clear and concise question on a new referendum on sovereignty.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._22-14) Chrétien defended the Clarity Act and attacked sovereigntist Quebec premier and former Bloc Québécois leader [Lucien Bouchard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucien_Bouchard "Lucien Bouchard"), challenging him to hold another referendum on sovereignty under the new laws, as Chrétien expected that the sovereigntists would lose such a referendum.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._22-14) The Liberal Party promised a number of government projects in Quebec to woo Quebec voters to the Liberal Party.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._22-14)

The Liberal Party appealed to Canada's most populous province of Ontario by acting to restore funding that its government had cut in the 1990s in order to cut the deficit of the 1990s.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._24-15) The Liberal government established a health accord with all premiers in September 2000 that involved major projected increases to public health care spending.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._24-15) Overall, the Liberals increased their number of seats in the House of Commons from 155 seats to 172 seats. They also won the popular vote in their former stronghold of Quebec for the first time since 1980, though they narrowly fell short of winning the most seats in the province, winning 36 seats to the Bloc's 38.

### Canadian Alliance

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2000_Canadian_federal_election&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section's source code: Canadian Alliance")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/e/ea/Canadian_Alliance_logo_-_logo_de_l%27Alliance_Canadienne.svg/250px-Canadian_Alliance_logo_-_logo_de_l%27Alliance_Canadienne.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Canadian_Alliance_logo_-_logo_de_l'Alliance_Canadienne.svg)

Canadian Alliance logo during the election.

The [Canadian Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Alliance "Canadian Alliance") (the common short form name of Canadian Reform Conservative Alliance) was a new political party in the election, having been created only months earlier as the successor to the [Reform Party of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Party_of_Canada "Reform Party of Canada"), a party founded as a [Western Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Canada "Western Canada") protest party which sought to become a national party in the 1990s.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._59-16) Reform Party leader [Preston Manning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preston_Manning "Preston Manning") was deeply disappointed with the Reform Party's failure to spread eastward in the 1997 election, as the Reform Party lost its only seat in Ontario in that election.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._60-17) Reform identified vote-splitting with its rival conservative movement, the Progressive Conservative Party as the cause for the Liberals' 1997 election victory, and Manning proposed the solution of a merger of the Reform and Progressive Conservative parties.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-18) This agenda by the Reform Party to unite the two parties was called the [United Alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Alternative "United Alternative") which began in 1998, and ultimately resulted in the Alliance.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-19)

The new party subsequently elected [Stockwell Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockwell_Day "Stockwell Day") as leader over Manning. The Alliance had hoped to use the 2000 election to eclipse the PC party in Ontario and Eastern Canada.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._59-16) The Alliance dedicated its campaign to demonstrating that the party was a national party and not as western-based as its predecessor had been perceived as.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._59-16) Day's more media friendly and "easy going" persona was expected to appeal to more [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario") voters than Manning's reputation as a [policy wonk](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/policy%20wonk "wikt:policy wonk"), and after the United Alternative project had integrated the successful [Provincial PCs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Conservative_Party_of_Ontario "Progressive Conservative Party of Ontario") in the party, the [Canadian Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Alliance "Canadian Alliance") was hoping for major improvements.

The Alliance campaigned on: cutting taxes by reducing the Federal taxation rate to two lower tax brackets, an end to the federal gun registration program, and importance of family values. The campaign was dogged by accusations: introducing a [two-tier health care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-tier_health_care "Two-tier health care")—the party would allow private health care to exist alongside the public medicare system; and for threatening the protection of gay rights and abortion rights. The latter accusations tended to focus on the party's residual[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_][direct democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_democracy "Direct democracy") provisions in their platform. The accusations against his party platform, along with Day's relative inexperience compared to decades-experienced fixtures like Clark and Chrétien, led to the party fading from contention.

While they did not force the Liberals into minority government, they did retain their official opposition status, and increased their numbers in the House of Commons by six seats, from 60 to 66. The Alliance ended up winning only two Ontario ridings. On election night, controversy arose when a CBC producer's gratuitously [sexist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexism "Sexism") comment about Stockwell Day's daughter-in-law, [Juliana Thiessen-Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juliana_Thiessen-Day "Juliana Thiessen-Day"), was accidentally broadcast on the Canadian networks' pooled election feed from Day's riding.

### Bloc Québécois

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2000_Canadian_federal_election&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section's source code: Bloc Québécois")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/c/c8/Bloc_Quebecois_B_logo_1990s.svg/250px-Bloc_Quebecois_B_logo_1990s.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bloc_Quebecois_B_logo_1990s.svg)

Logo of the Bloc Québécois during the election.

The Bloc Québécois suffered from the unpopular decision of its provincial counterpart, the ruling [Parti Québécois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parti_Qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois "Parti Québécois") government's agenda to merge the communities surrounding Quebec City into one community.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-20) Many [Québécois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French-speaking_Quebecer "French-speaking Quebecer") were angered by this decision and voted in protest against the Bloc or chose not to vote at all to demonstrate their frustration.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-21) Bloc leader [Gilles Duceppe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilles_Duceppe "Gilles Duceppe") received negative media attention after he decided to personally appoint candidate Noël Tremblay to run in the riding of [Chicoutimi—Le Fjord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicoutimi%E2%80%94Le_Fjord "Chicoutimi—Le Fjord") in spite of the Bloc's riding association's selection of [Sylvain Gaudreault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvain_Gaudreault "Sylvain Gaudreault") to run in the riding.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-22) The Bloc's 177 page platform was criticized as being far too large, thus few copies were distributed, few internet users accessed the platform, and it was rarely discussed during the campaign.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-23) Instead, the Bloc produced large numbers of copies of small booklets that outlined the policies within the large platform.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._145-24) The Bloc campaigned to try to win over previous supporters of the PC Party.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._145-24) This campaign strategy failed, as the Bloc lost seats to the Liberal Party due to the collapse of Quebec support for the Progressive Conservative Party, whose voters shifted to the Liberal Party.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-25) The Bloc won in 38 ridings, six ridings fewer than in the 1997 election.

### New Democratic Party

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2000_Canadian_federal_election&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section's source code: New Democratic Party")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/0/04/NDP_NPD_2000.svg/500px-NDP_NPD_2000.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NDP_NPD_2000.svg)

Logo of the New Democratic Party during the election.

The New Democratic Party suffered badly in the campaign due to the drop in support for the provincial New Democratic parties over the preceding decade and amid a scandal in 2000 facing [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia")'s NDP Premier [Glen Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glen_Clark "Glen Clark") who was forced to resign as Premier.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._114-26) Matters were made worse for the federal NDP after Saskatchewan's NDP Premier [Roy Romanow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Romanow "Roy Romanow") resigned in 2000 after the party lost seats in the 1999 Saskatchewan provincial election, and afterwards suggested that the federal NDP should merge with the Liberal Party.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._114-26) In Nova Scotia, the provincial NDP lost seats in its 1999 election while the NDP government of the Yukon had been recently defeated.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._114-26) As Canada's major [social democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_democracy "Social democracy") political party, it relied on support from the labour movement, but recent strains between the NDP and the [Canadian Auto Workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Auto_Workers "Canadian Auto Workers") union and the [Canadian Labour Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Labour_Congress "Canadian Labour Congress") had weakened the party's base of support.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._114-26) The party had received little media attention during the election and 2000 as a whole, due to the media's focus on Canada's newest political party, the [Canadian Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Alliance "Canadian Alliance"), the political comeback of former Prime Minister [Joe Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Clark "Joe Clark") to the leadership of the Progressive Conservative Party, and the leadership feud within the Liberal Party between Jean Chrétien and [Paul Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Martin "Paul Martin").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._115-10) The NDP did not expect to do well in the election and aimed to win thirty-two "must-win" seats.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._115-10)

The NDP's platform and campaign focused on protecting medicare while attacking the Liberal Party for its tax cuts to wealthy Canadians and corporations.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._122-4) The NDP's focus on attacking the Liberals failed to recognize the surging support for the Canadian Alliance in the province of Saskatchewan, where the NDP had hoped to gain seats.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-27) The NDP failed to galvanize support, as it remained low in support in polling results throughout most of the election campaign.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-28) NDP leader [Alexa McDonough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexa_McDonough "Alexa McDonough") performed badly in the French-language debate due to her not being fluent in French.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._128-29) In the English-language debate, McDonough attacked Alliance leader Stockwell Day for favouring two-tier health care and attacked Liberal leader Jean Chrétien for giving out tax cuts to the wealthy rather than funding Canada's public health care system.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election#cite_note-Dornan,_Christopher_Pp._128-29)

The Progressive Conservative Party aimed to regain its former place in Canadian politics under the leadership of former Prime Minister [Joe Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Clark "Joe Clark"). The [PC Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Conservative_Party_of_Canada "Progressive Conservative Party of Canada") had a very disappointing election, recording its lowest ever share of the national vote, falling from 20 to 12 seats, and being almost exclusively confined to the [Maritime provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_provinces "Maritime provinces"). **Oakville** was a federal [electoral district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_district_(Canada) "Electoral district (Canada)") in [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario"), Canada, that was represented in the [House of Commons of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_Canada "House of Commons of Canada") from 1997 to 2025.

After the [2022 Canadian federal electoral redistribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Canadian_federal_electoral_redistribution "2022 Canadian federal electoral redistribution"), the riding was abolished and divided into [Oakville East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakville_East "Oakville East") and [Oakville West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakville_West "Oakville West") for the [2025 Canadian federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Canadian_federal_election "2025 Canadian federal election").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oakville_(federal_electoral_district)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

It was created in 1996 from parts of [Halton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halton_(federal_electoral_district) "Halton (federal electoral district)") and [Oakville—Milton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakville%E2%80%94Milton "Oakville—Milton") ridings.

It consisted initially of the part of the Town of [Oakville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakville,_Ontario "Oakville, Ontario") lying southeast of the Queen Elizabeth Way and Upper Middle Road.

In 2003, it was redefined to consist of the part of the Town of Oakville lying southeast of a line drawn from the northeastern town limit southwest along Dundas Street East, southeast along Eighth Line and southwest along Upper Middle Road to the southwestern town limit. This riding was unchanged after the [2012 electoral redistribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_federal_electoral_redistribution,_2012 "Canadian federal electoral redistribution, 2012").

The current boundaries include the neighbourhoods of Lakeshore Woods, Bronte, Hopedale, Coronation Park, Kerr Village, Old Oakville, Eastlake, Glen Abbey, College Park, Iroquois Ridge, Clearview, and Joshua Creek.

2000: 1st Liberal 47.75% (23,073 votes), 2nd Alliance 27.99% (13,524), 3rd Progressive Conservative 19.85% (9,594). Vote share difference 1st-3rd = 47.75 - 19.85 = 27.90 percentage points.

2004: 1st Liberal 52.01% (28,729 votes), 2nd Conservative 35.35% (19,524), 3rd NDP 7.29% (4,027). Difference 52.01-7.29=44.72.

2006: 1st Liberal 43.35% (25,892), 2nd Conservative 42.10% (25,148), 3rd NDP 9.74% (5,815). Diff 43.35-9.74=33.61.

For 2008, winner was Conservative (26,011). 1st: 46.98% (26,011), 2nd: Liberal 37.08% (20,528), 3rd: Green 8.46% (4,681). Diff 46.98-8.46=38.52.

2011: Winner Conservative 51.65% (30,068), second Liberal 30.73% (17,890), third NDP 13.94% (8,117). Diff 51.65-13.94=37.71.

2015: Winner Liberal 49.39% (31,956), second Conservative 42.50% (27,497), third NDP 5.92% (3,830). Diff 49.39-5.92=43.47.

2019: Winner Liberal 46.28% (30,265), second Conservative 39.08% (25,561), third NDP 7.54% (4,928). Diff 46.28-7.54=38.74.

2021: Winner Liberal 46.1% (28,137), second Conservative 40.0% (24,430), third NDP 8.8% (5,373). Diff 46.1-8.8=37.3.

So largest difference is 44.72 in 2004 (Liberal vs NDP). Wait 44.72 > 43.47(2015). 2004 diff 44.72. Also check 2008 diff 38.52 etc.

Thus election with biggest difference is 2004. Runner up votes: Conservative 19,524 votes.

But check that there are ties? 2004 1st-liberal 28,729, 2nd-conservative 19,524. So runner up votes=19,524.
